title: Dropout
matchup: Hinton et al. (2012) and Srivastava et al. (2014) vs Hanson (1990)
question: Does the relationship between dropout and Hanson's 1990 stochastic delta rule support Schmidhuber's claim of an earlier invention?

usual_credit.summary: Dropout, which randomly omits hidden units during training to reduce overfitting, is usually credited to Geoffrey Hinton and his co-authors Nitish Srivastava, Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Ruslan Salakhutdinov, in a 2012 preprint and a 2014 paper in the Journal of Machine Learning Research. It was used in the AlexNet system that won the 2012 ImageNet competition, and Hinton's 2025 Nobel lecture credits the 2014 paper with the method.

claim.summary: Schmidhuber says that dropout is a variant of the stochastic delta rule that Stephen José Hanson published in 1990, a stochastic way of training networks by backpropagation, and that Hinton's 2012 papers and a later patent did not cite it. He makes the same point about the 2021 Turing Lecture by LeCun, Bengio and Hinton, which cites Hinton (2012) for dropout without mentioning Hanson.

response.summary: The dropout papers motivate random unit omission as a way to prevent co-adaptation and overfitting, while the 2014 paper's related-work section discusses denoising autoencoders and noise in hidden states. They do not cite Hanson (1990). Frazier-Logue and Hanson's 2018 preprint, later published in Neural Computation, argues that dropout is a special case of the stochastic delta rule, whose weights have means and standard deviations. That comparison supplies an explicit argument for the earlier method's relationship to dropout, but it is not a reply from Hinton or his co-authors accepting or rejecting the missing-citation complaint.

agreed_facts: Hanson published 'A stochastic version of the delta rule' in Physica D in 1990.

Hinton and co-authors posted 'Improving neural networks by preventing co-adaptation of feature detectors' to arXiv on 3 July 2012, and Srivastava and colleagues published their dropout paper in the Journal of Machine Learning Research in 2014.
Neither the 2012 preprint nor the 2014 journal paper lists Hanson (1990) among its references.
Krizhevsky, Sutskever and Hinton used dropout in their 2012 ImageNet paper and cited the 2012 preprint for it.
Frazier-Logue and Hanson's 2018 preprint states that dropout is a special case of the stochastic delta rule.
crux: The dispute is whether dropout, which silences each hidden unit at random with a fixed probability and rescales at test time, is a special case of the stochastic delta rule, in which each weight is a random variable with a learned mean and standard deviation, or a separate technique with a different motivation. It also asks whether the 2012 authors owed a citation to the 1990 paper.

card.headline: Dropout
card.question: Is dropout a variant of Hanson's 1990 stochastic delta rule or a separate technique?
card.claim: He says dropout is a variant of Hanson's 1990 stochastic delta rule, which Hinton's 2012 papers and the 2021 Turing Lecture did not cite.
card.pushback: Hinton's group has not answered, and dropout silences units at a fixed rate while Hanson's rule makes each weight random with learned mean and spread.
card.crux: The question is whether silencing random units at a fixed rate is a special case of making weights random with learned spread.
